4. Under Order 41, rule 5(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellate Court may on sufficient cause order stay of execution of a decree or order appealed against. Order 41 rule 5(3) provides that the Court must be satisfied on 3 points before it can issue such an order for stay. Order 41, rule 5(4) provide that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (3), the Court can make an ex-parte order for stay of execution pending the bearing of the application. 

 6. In the aforecited case petitioner Hiralal obtained an order from the trial Court to issue a writ of delivery of possession on 18-6-23 in execution of a decree for ejectment of the opposite party Chuni Sao. On 19-6-23 the opposite party preferred an appeal against the decree before the District Judge of Gays and on the same day he made an application before the District Judge praying for stay of delivery of possession pending the hearing of the appeal. The District Judge passed the following order: 

 7. On the following day i.e. the 20th June 1923 the opposite party filed another application before the District Judge, complaining that the order of stay was communicated to the peon but the peon put the decree holder in possession and dispossessed the judgment-debtor. The learned District Judge stayed execution of the decree pending disposal of the appeal and declared that the delivery of possession executed yesterday was invalid. 

 8. The Petitioner Hiralal stated before the Patna High Court that he took delivery of possession of the suit house on 19-6-23 at 9 am. before he was aware of the ad-interim order of stay. It is in these circumstances that the Patna High Court decided that the learned District Judge in dealing with the applications dated the 19th and 20th June has proceeded ex parte without giving any notice to the decree-holder. The Patna High Court has held that before an order of stay is passed under Order 41, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure it is necessary that notice of the application "should" be given to the decree holder and he "should" be called upon to show cause why execution should not be stayed. The Patna High Court ordered that the order for stay of execution passed on the 19th June will be treated as an ad-interim order till the disposal of the application. The decree-holder-petitioner shall be at liberty to show cause why the execution should not be stayed. 

 (b) that the application has been made without unreasonable delay; and (c) that security has been given by the applicant for the due performance of such decree or order as may ultimately be binding upon him. 

 11. It is clear that none of the three conditions relate to the respondent. These are matters between the appellant and the Court. While hearing the stay matter, however, if the Court finds that the respondent needs to be heard because, for example, some steps might already have been taken for execution of the decree, the Court may issue a notice to the respondent to show cause why an order of stay of execution shall not be passed, but essentially it is for the Court to be satisfied on these three points and in each case it is for the Court to decide whether the satisfaction will be arrived at after hearing only the appellant or after hearing the respondent as well. It cannot be laid down as an inflexible rule that under all circumstances the respondent must be heard before a final order of stay of execution can be granted to the appellant. The Patna High Court speaks in terms of should', not in terms of 'must'. 

 12. I do not think that the meaning of Order 41, rules 5(4) is that the Court may make an ex-parte order for stay of execution, but before passing a final order of the application the respondent must be heard. Sub-rule (4) clearly means that before final disposal of the appellant's application for stay the Court may make an ex-parte order for stay of execution. The Court may or may not hear the respondent when the appellant's application is finally heard and disposed of. Whether the Court will at all hear the respondent and when and under what circumstances the Court will hear him may best be left to the discretion of the Court which will, of course, be guided by judicial consideration. Even when the respondent is not heard, the Court will always bear in mind that the respondent cannot be denied the fruit of his decree without sufficient cause.
